title: Juxtaposing Legal AI Tools and their Practical Use: A Qualitative Study
pub: AI for Access to Justice Workshop, International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law 2025
author: Juraj Vladika · Stephen Meisenbacher · Benedikt Thiess · Florian Matthes

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused framing and materially extends it with qualitative evidence that reliable adoption depends on workflow redesign, systems integration, procurement, compliance and clear organisational ownership—not model capability alone. Its participant accounts identify barriers rather than measuring resulting service quality or productivity.
qs: Additionally, A2 reported that beyond technical systems, introducing new tools may disrupt established routines, requiring changes in the way one approaches legal work.
Furthermore, two providers noted that in some law firms there is a lack of an appropriate contact person in charge of introducing legal AI solutions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with direct provider–applier interview evidence. It documents human verification as the dominant reliability safeguard and shows that integration, legacy systems, workflow disruption and provider-user alignment—not model functionality alone—shape practical value. Its findings are perceptual and geographically limited rather than causal performance evidence.
qs: A highly important factor in ensuring reliability of Legal AI was the need for human verification – mentioned in 24 out of 25 interviews.

We find that aspects such as tool integration is perceived as equally important as functionality, where factors such as regional differences (in legal systems) and considerations of (legacy) systems in law firms are deciding factors in user satisfaction with AI.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s core balance: legal AI may improve access to legal knowledge and efficiency, but should function primarily as an expert-supported tool with human validation. Its evidence is qualitative and perception-based, so it does not establish improved legal outcomes or directly examine how risks fall on unrepresented users.
qs: Access to Justice is Access to Legal Knowledge We find that perceived benefits of Legal AI tools, both from the perspective of providers and appliers, relate to increasing access to legal knowledge and improving the efficiency of legal work.

Additionally, there was a near unanimous sentiment that human validation is paramount the development and deployment of these tools; moreover, the “human element” and need for domain expertise was often stressed.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The study aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that Legal AI primarily supports rather than replaces legal professionals and that effective adoption depends on human expertise, trust, onboarding and education. Its evidence is qualitative and geographically limited, and it does not directly establish productivity gains or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Interestingly, while providers (P5, P10, P11) envisioned AI ultimately to replace much of today’s legal work, a larger number of interviewees (five providers, two appliers) explicitly mentioned their belief that AI will not replace much of the work of legal professionals, but play a support role.
In addition, these          interviewees stress the need for expert-based evaluation, i.e., to “ask the right questions” (A9).

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s central proposition by reporting that interviewees anticipated both task substitution and predominantly supportive AI use, without establishing aggregate employment effects. It also reinforces the continuing role of human trust and expert evaluation as limits on full substitution.
qs: Interestingly, while providers (P5, P10, P11) envisioned AI ultimately to replace much of today’s legal work, a larger number of interviewees (five providers, two appliers) explicitly mentioned their belief that AI will not replace much of the work of legal professionals, but play a support role.
• The necessity of human input: P2, P5, A6, and A9 emphasize that the entirety of legal work is          based on trust, and ethically speaking, it would be unwise to rely fully on AI.

kp.k: Interview evidence captures adoption experiences, not market-wide outcomes
kp.d: The study compares 15 Legal AI tool providers and 9 appliers in the German-speaking region, recruited through LinkedIn over three months. Interviews were conducted in German via Zoom and analysed through iterative qualitative coding and constant comparison. Participants averaged 9.88 years of experience and generally held higher management positions. The authors acknowledge geographic limits, potentially subjective coding and desirability bias; the findings concern participants’ reported experiences and perceptions.
qs: Over the course of three months, we recruited 24 interviewees: 15 fitting the provider role and 9 fitting the applier role.
All interviews were conducted in German and via Zoom.

Finally, our interviewee pool is threatened by desirability bias, where the interview data and their derived findings are based on the information our interviewees chose to present to us, and may not always capture the complete picture.

kp.k: Providers and users align on efficiency and knowledge access
kp.d: Both groups identify faster access to legal knowledge, time savings and easier familiarisation with documents as central benefits. Efficiency appeared in all but one applier interview. Reported applications include processing more documents, summarisation, relevance filtering and knowledge management; one applier reported lower personnel costs and another described discovering otherwise difficult-to-obtain insights. These are interview-based perceived benefits rather than measured productivity effects.
qs: Both sides cite efficiency and access to legal knowledge as the primary drivers for using Legal AI tools.
When talking to appliers, it was interesting to observe that a large focus was also placed on efficiency as a primary benefit, mentioned in all but one applier interview.
Relatedly, appliers explicitly mention the ability to process more documents in less time (AB4), as well as lower personnel costs (AB7), as important factors.

kp.k: Tool markets extend beyond law firms
kp.d: Law firms were the most frequently mentioned customers, with 11 mentions. Providers also identified public institutions and notaries, each mentioned twice, and private companies in other sectors and large-company legal departments, each mentioned three times. Providers associated adoption with time pressure, manual work, personnel shortages and document volumes. Appliers additionally cited client demand and improving public appearance, alongside operational needs.
qs: Other groups within the legal industry include public institutions (e.g., courts and government organizations) and notaries, each mentioned twice.
Outside of legal firms, providers’ tools are also used by private companies in other sectors such as finance and by legal departments of big companies, both mentioned three times.

Some appliers provided additional insights for AI adoption: boosting knowledge management (A9), asking questions about documents (A6), identifying use cases for their company (A1), client demand (A2, A8), and improving public appearance (A2, A3).

kp.k: Legal AI combines language models with other methods
kp.d: Nine of 15 providers mentioned GPT-4 hosted on Azure as their product backbone. Other proprietary and open-source models also appeared. Providers described combining LLMs with named entity recognition, semantic search, pattern matching and statistical methods, rather than treating LLMs as complete solutions. P4 reported difficulties with GPT’s in-depth legal knowledge and reasoning.
qs: The most popular is GPT-4 hosted on the Azure Cloud, as mentioned by 9 out of 15 providers (P2–4, 9–10, 12–15).
Despite GPT’s popularity, P4 mentioned how it can struggle with in-depth legal knowledge and reasoning.
Interviewees expressed that LLMs alone aren’t a fix-all solution, but many providers combine them with more standard NLP methods.

kp.k: Human verification remains central despite technical reliability measures
kp.d: Providers described symbolic rules, decision trees and retrieval-augmented generation as reliability approaches; RAG was mentioned five times. Isolated environments and ISO certifications were also presented as trust measures, while two providers lacked a reliability method. Human checking, correction and final decision-making were treated as paramount. The paper reports this in '24 out of 25 interviews', despite describing a 24-interview study elsewhere; that inconsistency should not be silently corrected.
qs: Another popular approach for increasing reliability, mentioned five times, is Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), which grounds LLM responses in client-provided documents.
Additionally, two providers advertised ISO certifications, while two others lack a method to ensure reliability.
A highly important factor in ensuring reliability of Legal AI was the need for human verification – mentioned in 24 out of 25 interviews.
This refers to the process of legal practitioners verifying and correcting AI model outputs, steering the way the tool is applied, and always making the final decisions.

kp.k: Regular use coexists with unmet expectations
kp.d: Five of nine appliers reported daily use, and eight intended to continue; the remaining applier had a one-time solution. Three reported that capabilities matched expectations because they had selected tools for specific use cases, while four reported incomplete fulfilment of expectations. Some expected extensive out-of-the-box automation that did not materialise. Provider P1 described a shift over the preceding two years from managing fear of AI to managing rising expectations.
qs: The majority of interviewed appliers (5/9) said that they are using their Legal AI tool on a daily basis.

Virtually all appliers (8/9) said they would also continue using the tool in the future, while one applier (A4) mentioned that the tool was designed for their company as a one-time use solution for a specific problem.
Similarly, three other appliers mentioned how they expected the developed tool to solve all their problems out-of-the-box and automate a great deal of their work, which was not realized.
This finding is further confirmed by provider P1, who indicates a shift in the last two years from managing clients’ fear about AI to managing their growing expectations.

kp.k: Users differ over general-purpose versus specialised tools
kp.d: Three providers reported client requests for tools covering all needs to avoid switching between systems. Four providers instead reported preferences for specialised tools offering better task-specific accuracy. The authors identify this unresolved difference as a provider–applier alignment problem, alongside communication difficulties between technical and legal professionals. Five providers stressed including a legal professional during development, and five emphasised close collaboration after deployment.
qs: Three providers (P3, P8, P11) mentioned how their clients requested a Legal AI tool that would cover all their needs because shuffling between multiple tools gets overwhelming.

On the other hand, four providers (P1, P2, P5, P12) argued that their customers preferred using specialized tools that perform well on specific legal tasks rather than using a general-purpose tool with poorer accuracy.
Therefore, five providers underlined the need to have a legal professional on the team during the tool development.
Additionally, five providers stressed the importance of close collaboration with the users after the tool is deployed, since this can lead to the discovery of new use cases or needs.

kp.k: Workflow fit and integration shape user satisfaction
kp.d: Appliers valued onboarding, usable interfaces, affordable prices, legal-style text, predefined prompts, provider communication and Microsoft Word integration. Unmet needs included follow-up dialogue, awareness of local laws, better table structuring, extraction from legal forms, internal document-management integration and individual workflow customisation. Two appliers wanted more automated tool testing and evaluation. The authors recommend stronger communication, onboarding and education, treating integration as equally important as functionality.
qs: Additionally, two appliers indicated a desire for more automation in terms of tool testing and evaluation.
Finally, two appliers mentioned that their employees wanted a higher level of customization and tailoring the tool for their individual workflow.

We find that aspects such as tool integration is perceived as equally important as functionality, where factors such as regional differences (in legal systems) and considerations of (legacy) systems in law firms are deciding factors in user satisfaction with AI.

kp.k: Procurement, confidentiality and billing incentives constrain adoption
kp.d: Seven providers identified sales cycles lasting at least two years, with compliance requirements and complex procurement, as a major customer-acquisition challenge. Five reported AI scepticism tied to error liability and client confidentiality. Appliers described integration difficulties, disruption of established routines, data-protection obstacles and personal reluctance. Two providers reported missing organisational contacts responsible for adoption; two others expressed the view that some practitioners resist efficiency because it reduces billable hours.
qs: numerous compliance requirements and a complex procurement process.
Another obstacle mentioned by five providers is general skepticism towards AI, usually tied to the challenges of error liability and client confidentiality.
Furthermore, two providers noted that in some law firms there is a lack of an appropriate contact person in charge of introducing legal AI solutions.
An interesting opinion coming from other two providers is that some legal practitioners are not interested in higher efficiency because it decreases their billable hours.

kp.k: Training data and legacy infrastructure impede development
kp.d: Seven providers reported difficulty acquiring training data, citing insufficient anonymised data, data-quality problems and limited generalisability across clients. Six identified interfacing with law-firm systems as a primary technical challenge. Providers described legacy software lacking modern APIs, while an applier noted third-party data management as an additional complication.
qs: Firstly, an often-recurring theme amongst the providers was the challenge of training data, where seven providers mentioned difficulties in acquiring training data.
The primary underlying reasons for the challenge were given as lack of anonymized data, challenges in the existence of quality data, and lack of generalizability from one client’s use to another.
Six providers pointed to another primary technical challenge: interfacing with law firm systems.
P3 mentions difficulties in connecting with these systems, which rarely have modern APIs.

kp.k: Workforce predictions favour support but remain divided
kp.d: Three providers envisioned AI eventually replacing much current legal work, whereas five providers and two appliers explicitly expected a support role rather than substantial replacement. Participants supporting augmentation cited overloaded firms, trust, human expertise and professional restrictions. P9 predicted more attractive, higher-level roles. These are participants’ expectations and arguments, not measured employment outcomes; the discussion of restrictions is region-specific and refers to 'anwaltliches Berufsrecht'.
qs: Interestingly, while providers (P5, P10, P11) envisioned AI ultimately to replace much of today’s legal work, a larger number of interviewees (five providers, two appliers) explicitly mentioned their belief that AI will not replace much of the work of legal professionals, but play a support role.
P15 and A9 argue that since law firms are already overloaded with work, fears of unemployment are unfounded.
P2, P5, A6, and A9 emphasize that the entirety of legal work is based on trust, and ethically speaking, it would be unwise to rely fully on AI.

kp.k: Access-to-justice gains are argued through improved service
kp.d: The authors connect practitioners’ reported improvements in knowledge access and efficiency to potential access-to-justice benefits: better service, reduced backlogs and quicker, more informed legal assistance. Two providers also identified publishing more anonymised court verdicts as a transparency benefit. The access-to-justice connection is an authorial argument drawn from professional-use interviews, rather than a reported measurement of reduced unmet civil legal need.
qs: In this, we draw an important connection between the improved access to legal knowledge reported by legal professionals in our interviews, to the general improvement of access to justice.
With the two main perceived benefits of access to knowledge and efficiency, Legal AI tools can help to reduce backlogs in the legal pipeline, thus affording quicker and more informed legal services.
Additionally, two providers see transparency as a major benefit of Legal AI, such as in enabling the publication of more anonymized court verdicts (PB8).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors report perceived efficiency and knowledge-access benefits, persistent gaps between tools and user needs, and competing interviewee predictions about workforce substitution versus support.
pts.d: The authors synthesise provider and applier reports that Legal AI speeds document processing, summarisation, familiarisation and access to legal knowledge. A5 reports lower personnel costs; A6 reports enhanced discovery of insights. These are reported experiences and perceptions rather than measured productivity effects. The authors further argue that better knowledge access and efficiency can improve service quality and reduce legal backlogs, connecting these benefits to access to justice; they do not document reductions in unmet civil legal need. Workforce predictions are explicitly divided: P5, P10 and P11 envision AI ultimately replacing much current legal work, whereas five providers and two appliers envisage primarily a support role. P15 and A9 argue that overloaded firms need relief rather than replacement, and P9 predicts more attractive legal roles. The authors also find that tools often fall short of expectations and workflow requirements. Two providers report that some practitioners resist efficiency because it reduces billable hours. These are interviewee views, not an established market-wide effect.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of a qualitative interview study of 15 providers and nine appliers in the German-speaking region, not performance benchmarks, causal estimates or labour-market measurements.
pts.d: The authors recruited through LinkedIn and conducted German-language Zoom interviews, analysing transcripts through iterative open and axial coding and constant comparison. Participants averaged 9.88 years of experience and generally held senior positions. Eight of nine appliers mentioned efficiency benefits; five reported daily use and eight intended continued use. Four appliers reported that tools did not fully meet expectations. The workforce outlook is based on interviewees' beliefs, while the access-to-justice connection is the authors' interpretation of reported knowledge and efficiency benefits. The authors acknowledge geographic limitations, subjective coding and desirability bias. Their reliability section reports human verification in '24 out of 25 interviews', inconsistent with the stated total of 24; the qualitative conclusion is near-unanimous support for human checking, but that denominator cannot be reconciled from the document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported benefits concern existing use at the time of the 2025 study; future workforce and justice effects have no fixed forecast horizon and depend on human oversight, integration and adoption conditions.
pts.d: Recruitment occurred over three months, but calendar dates for the interviews are not supplied. P1 describes a shift over the preceding two years from managing fear of AI to managing expectations. Replacement is described as occurring 'ultimately', without a date; continued-use intentions likewise lack a specified horizon. The authors present human verification and final practitioner decisions as central conditions for reliable use. Interviewees identify confidentiality, liability, data protection, professional regulation, procurement, reluctance to change and legacy-system integration as constraints. Seven providers describe sales cycles lasting at least two years. The paper calls 'anwaltliches Berufsrecht' labour law for lawyers; its reported constraint concerns region-specific professional rules, not a demonstrated universal prohibition on automation. Providers disagree about demand for general-purpose versus specialised tools. The authors recommend better communication, onboarding and education as prerequisites for broader adoption rather than promising inevitable uptake.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are legal-AI software vendors and professional users, principally law firms; in-house departments, public institutions, notaries and clients are also implicated.
pts.d: Providers are tool vendors, not identified as alternative legal service providers delivering legal work. They report law firms as the principal customer group, with 11 mentions; public institutions and notaries receive two mentions each, while private companies in other sectors and large-company legal departments receive three each. Practitioners are affected through reduced repetitive work, faster knowledge retrieval and document processing, continuing verification duties and changed routines. Firms face integration, procurement and confidentiality requirements and potentially lower personnel costs; some interviewees foresee substitution, others relief of understaffed or overloaded teams. Vendors face training-data shortages, long sales cycles and mismatches between product design and user workflows. Clients and the public are potential indirect beneficiaries of quicker, better-informed service and publication of anonymised judgments. The study does not directly measure benefits for individuals or small organisations unable to obtain legal help, nor does it establish changes in associate leverage, staffing shapes or profession-wide employment.
